prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory, showing how exporting decisions and reallocation across firms shape the gains from trade

statement.case_for: My preferred part is unchanged, but I have re-examined it against the chair's questions. The discovery is a change in the unit of analysis in trade, from the industry to the firm. Melitz (2003) is a single, identifiable originating model in which productivity differences drive selection into exporting, reallocation across firms and a new channel for the gains from trade. Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus foreign direct investment is a separable extension by the same originator and a co-author. The qualitative predictions (selection into exporting, exporter premia, reallocation) have been examined in firm-level data from many countries for more than twenty years, as far as I know from the literature and from colleagues' statements. I have not verified this independently. On the chair's adjacency question, I would count a neighbouring prize against a candidate only when the earlier citation covered the same discovery. The 2008 prize covered increasing returns and earlier new trade theory, and selection on firm productivity is a later and different mechanism. It also has no thematic overlap with the 2024 prize on institutions. On the credit boundary, I would accept a citation worded around the theory of selection and the gains from trade, and I would not claim the whole firm-level trade agenda. That wording does not reduce what Melitz and Helpman are credited with. It states the boundary honestly. The fact that five members name the same pair is not merit evidence for me, and I do not use it as such. My ordering rests on the sharpness of attribution, maturity, and the absence of same-discovery overlap.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains attribution. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum contributed closely related empirical and quantitative work that a two-name award cannot credit, and Redding's quantitative extensions are also left out. A citation framed around the theory narrows the problem but does not remove it. Parts of the field would contest the boundary. The welfare magnitudes depend on functional-form assumptions (Pareto productivity, CES demand), so the mechanism is better established than the size of the gains. Trade would receive a second prize after 2008, which some members may weigh. I also withdraw a point from round 1: I said Helpman's record appears under another ballot item, but on the supplied shortlist he is credited only on B044, so I cannot support that as an uncertainty. A final difficulty is that no ballot has six supporters in round 1, so my preferred part may not carry. I do not treat that as a reason to move to another part without a merit-based reason.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B037 with Kiyotaki and Moore, a clean two-author origin that is about three decades old. He accepts that the empirical evidence for the collateral channel is largely indirect and that the 2022 overlap is unchecked. He lists B044 as his first alternative and says the gap around Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum keeps him from ranking it first.
responses.response: I agree that B037 has the cleaner attribution of the two. That is a real strength and it is why I now list it as an alternative, replacing B017. I am moving B037 up because the 2022 overlap is partial and not duplication, and Hassler and Strömberg make a persuasive case that the mechanism disciplined later work. On the gap you cite, I would not call it unresolved. Bernard and Jensen documented the exporter facts that the Melitz model explains, and Eaton-Kortum is a Ricardian strand with a different mechanism. A citation on the theory of selection and the gains from trade therefore leaves those contributions adjacent and not displaced. I still place B044 first, because the core predictions have been tested directly in firm-level micro data, whereas the collateral channel rests more on calibrated models. Neither of us has checked the 2022 scientific background, so that overlap remains an open question for both.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B038 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. He reads the skill-premium, task and trade-shock strands as one question about how technology and trade shift labour demand, and he says that if the committee splits the strands, Dorn should displace Katz.
responses.response: The chair asked what would have to be resolved for B038 to become my preferred part, and your position helps answer it. I do not yet see it as one discovery. Your own caveats about Acemoglu's recognised work and the Dorn-or-Katz choice point to a boundary that is a judgement. What would move me is a committee definition of the achievement as empirical evidence on adjustment to trade shocks and technology in local labour markets, with Autor, Dorn and Hanson credited, plus a view that the persistence and identification debates concern magnitudes and not the finding. I agree with your conditional that Dorn should displace Katz if the strands are separated. I hold that conditional view with uncertainty, since I cannot verify the literature on persistence from the supplied evidence. If the committee keeps the broader definition, the trio you propose is the right one, but it brings the overlaps with Acemoglu, Goldin and Card into the case.

responses.point: Andersson prefers B038 with Autor, Hanson and Katz, and describes Autor and Hanson as a fallback he could accept if one strand is judged more ready than the other. He also argues the 2024 prize concerned institutions and not the task-based analysis, so the Acemoglu overlap is manageable.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of 2024. The 2024 prize concerned institutions and prosperity, and I would not treat it as the same discovery as the task framework. I would qualify the Autor-Hanson fallback. If the committee narrows the award to trade shocks, dropping Dorn from the central papers has no principled basis, and that is the weakest of the narrower options. Autor-Dorn-Hanson would follow the authorship of those papers, so I would support that form over Autor-Hanson. If instead it drops the trade strand, the award rests on Katz and Autor's skill-and-task work, with the overlap risk you describe. In either case I would want the citation to say which of Katz's contributions it recognises, as Strömberg suggests, since he also appears on B045.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson prefers B044 and separates the well-confirmed qualitative selection mechanism from the model-dependent welfare magnitudes. She would word the citation around the mechanism, would not add Redding as a third name, and says Helpman should be credited here for the firm-heterogeneity work with Melitz.
responses.response: I agree with all three points. The mechanism-versus-magnitudes distinction is the right way to handle the Pareto-CES criticism, and a citation about selection and reallocation does that. I also agree that Redding extended the framework and should not be a third name, and that Helpman's claim here rests on Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple. I would add one point on the cap. A two-name award leaves one unique-laureate slot unused, but I do not think Redding or any of the empirical contributors fills it without blurring the credit boundary, so I would not fill it. I also accept your honesty about the limit. Even a mechanism-centred citation acknowledges that Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum are close to the discovery and outside the two names.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a citation limited to the theory of selection and gains from trade, or whether parts of the field would still see the exclusion of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum as an under-crediting of the empirical foundation.
How far the gains-from-trade magnitudes survive alternative assumptions to Pareto productivity and CES demand. I rely on colleagues' statements and my own knowledge of the literature.

Whether B038 should be defined as one labour-demand achievement or as a trade-shock achievement, and whether the third slot is Katz or Dorn. I have no independent evidence to resolve that, and the persistence of the China-shock effects is still debated according to several members.
Whether the 2022 prize covers the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism closely enough to count against B037. Neither I nor the B037 supporters have checked its scientific background.

Whether my alternatives are ordered correctly. I replaced B017 with B037 mainly because of attribution clarity and absence of overlap with the 2024 prize. This is a modest weighting judgement and I have not independently verified citation or impact figures.
statement.conflict_note: Chair's question on the co-author named only 'Persson': the supplied profile lists 'Persson and Rothstein' (Governance) without a first name. From my own recollection, and not from any supplied evidence, this is Anna Persson of Gothenburg and not Torsten Persson of B017. I cannot confirm that from the permitted record, so I leave it for the committee as an unconfirmed identification. B017 is no longer among my alternatives, which reduces its relevance to my configuration. I still disclose my field proximity to B017 (political science, democratisation, institutions) and the fact that I gave the 2024 presentation speech on a neighbouring theme. The profile notes that such speeches may reflect collective drafting. The supplied profile documents no connection to Melitz, Helpman, Autor, Hanson, Katz, Dorn, Kiyotaki or Moore. I am a Stockholm University colleague of Hassler, Krusell and Boppart, in a different department. On the chair's question about limiting participation: I do not believe a disclosed tie requires me to limit participation on B044, B038 or B037, and conflicts are disclosed but not adjudicated.
